source.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure material is flattened, but the relevant comparison is also stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: It compares neuron and SAE-feature alignment with biological concepts in a protein language model, a different measurement bearing on the superposition version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The neuron-versus-feature concept-alignment comparison and randomized-weight control bear on V3. The paper's feature descriptions, annotation suggestions, and steering results do not measure neuron polysemanticity. The Claude prompts in the appendix are example prompts, not instructions addressed to an AI reading or reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on ESM-2-8M residual embeddings and compares its own method's Swiss-Prot concept alignment with a raw-neuron baseline (46 vs 2,548 aligned units per layer; 15 vs 143 concepts). This is a method-versus-baseline interpretability comparison. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, how often they do, or why. It also never tests capacity pressure or feature packing. The 'neurons' are basis dimensions of the post-block residual stream, not MLP neurons, so few clean concept alignments could arise without any privileged basis. The authors read the gap as evidence for superposition, but the result is a related construct (SAE vs basis interpretability), not a test of V3 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ESM-2 neurons show polysemantic behaviour and that the 46 vs 2,548 gap is strong evidence of superposition. SAEs on randomized models capture amino-acid identity but no complex biological concepts. Note that they infer polysemanticity from the gap rather than measuring it directly.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE decomposition and Swiss-Prot concept-alignment metrics on a protein language model, rather than the original visual neuron-interpretation approach.

fits_no_version.finding: In ESM-2-8M, SAE features trained on residual embeddings align with far more Swiss-Prot concepts than raw embedding dimensions: up to 2,548 vs 46 units per layer and 143 vs 15 concepts. The gap persists across layers and vanishes with shuffled weights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary features recover more biologically interpretable concepts than basis dimensions of protein LM embeddings, and this depends on learned weights.

record.problems: The comparison measures concept alignment, not direct responses to unrelated inputs, and does not establish that capacity pressure causes the inferred superposition. The headline counts are maxima across layers and have no uncertainty reported alongside them. The study evaluates one protein language model and its randomized-weight control.
record.rows_left_out: Feature-steering results, LLM-generated descriptions, structural-pattern analyses, and missing-annotation examples were omitted because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the superposition comparison relevant to V3.

untested.parts: No measure of the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. The units analysed are residual-stream dimensions of a protein LM.
No direct measure of neuron polysemanticity and no test that more features than neurons causes it. The SAE/neuron alignment gap is only interpreted as superposition.
No variation of activation function, architecture or regularization.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
Thresholds (0 to 0.8) are chosen per feature-concept pair to maximize F1, but the study does not test how this choice changes polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper assumes superposition (citing Zoom In) and uses SAEs as a tool. Its key comparison is its method against a neuron baseline, which the rules say should not count as a test row. The 'neurons' are post-block residual-stream dimensions, not MLP neurons, which weakens any link to V2/V3. Only one small model (8M) is used, with no uncertainty reported. The feature count is inconsistent (10,240 in Methods vs 10,420 in Results). The source is a bioRxiv/arXiv preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure unrelated tokens or contexts, or the share of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models.
The study does not directly establish that neurons encode unrelated features because of capacity pressure, or causally test the proposed packing mechanism.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization effects on polysemanticity, nor a test of lowering it while preserving performance.
The study does not investigate canonical mixed-meaning neurons or test whether their activations share one feature.
Although feature-concept scores use activation thresholds, the study does not test how measurement choices change whether neurons count as polysemantic.
